iOS for Android developers · Start here · 1 of 5

Frozen, not stopped

On Android, an app in the background keeps its process, and its threads can keep running. On iOS, a few seconds after the user leaves, your app stops running any code at all. Here's what that means for your work.

The problem

On Android, when the user switches away, your Activity is stopped, but your process lives on: a coroutine can finish its upload, a thread can keep writing to the database. You save state in onStop and the process might still run for a long time. Write the same app for iOS, and the upload dies a few seconds after the user leaves. What happens to an iOS app in the background?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

UIKit, Apple's framework that runs an iOS app's screens, keeps every app in one of a few app states: not running, inactive (in front but not taking touches, like during a phone call banner), active (in front, taking touches), background, and suspended.

The big difference from Android is the last step. When the user leaves, your app goes to the background and gets a few seconds to finish crucial work: the callback that announces it (sceneDidEnterBackground) has five seconds to return. Shortly after, iOS suspends the app: its memory stays, but none of its code runs, on any thread. No coroutine, no timer, nothing.

A suspended app can be woken up again when the user comes back, and resumes as if nothing happened. Or, when memory is needed, iOS ends it, and no code of yours runs at that moment. The "about to terminate" callback isn't called for a suspended app, so it can't be your chance to save.

So the iOS rule is: save as you enter the background, and if work truly must finish, say so. For a short task, beginBackgroundTask asks iOS for extra time before suspension. For uploads and downloads, a background session hands the transfer to iOS itself, which carries it on in a separate process even while your app is suspended or ended.

The analogy

On Android, the clerk from the house keeps working at a back desk after the shop closes, until the town hall decides to end it. On iOS, a few seconds after closing, the whole house is frozen in place: nobody moves until the owner returns, or until the house is quietly torn down. (Want something to continue? Hand it to the town's own courier service before you close.)

Check yourself

Your iOS app starts a 30-second upload in an ordinary session, and the user leaves the app after 5 seconds. You did nothing special. What happens?

Not quite. On iOS, a suspended app runs no code at all; the upload stops with it.

Right. Suspended means no code runs, on any thread.

Not quite. Suspension stops every thread of the app, not only the main one.

Why save state when entering the background, not when the app is about to be ended?

Not quite. It isn't slow: it never gets the chance to run.

Not quite. Frequency isn't the point: when a suspended app is ended, no code runs at all.

Right. No code runs when a suspended app is ended.

What's the difference between background and suspended?

Not quite. Both happen after the user leaves; the difference is whether your code runs.

Right. Briefly running vs not running.

Sources

  • Apple: Managing your app's life cycle ("When someone dismisses your app's UI, UIKit moves the associated scene to the background state and eventually to the suspended state. UIKit can disconnect a background or suspended scene at any time to reclaim its resources")
  • Apple: Extending your app's background execution time ("That method has five seconds to perform any tasks and return. Shortly after that method returns, iOS puts your app into the suspended state")
  • Apple: About the app launch sequence (iOS "suspends your process without allowing any application code to run")

What you now know

An iOS app moves through app states: not running, inactive, active, background, suspended. Seconds after it goes to the background it's suspended: still in memory, running no code. iOS can end a suspended app without running any of your code, so save your state as you enter the background, not at the end.
